title: Brokers and capabilities

story: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, has finished a step of RH-1234 and must push it to the branch nova/RH-1234. Pushing to GitHub needs a credential. The easy way is to put the GitHub App's token on the VM, the fresh machine Nova works on, and let git use it like on your laptop.

Now imagine that token on the VM on the day someone hides an instruction for agents in a ticket comment, and the model believes it. The token works for every repo the App is installed on and every branch the App may write, from any computer, until it expires. A fooled Nova could push to main in another repo, or paste the token into its PR, where anyone could copy it and use it from home.
hook.question: How can Nova push its branch and open its PR without ever holding a GitHub key?

p: Three things take part. The VM runs Nova and git. GitHub is where the code lives. Between them sits the broker, a small service of ours that holds the GitHub App's private key and makes every GitHub call for every run. The VM never talks to GitHub with a key of its own. It asks the broker, and the broker decides whether this run may do this thing, and only then does it.

What the VM holds instead is a capability. When a run starts, the orchestrator tells the broker what the run may touch: one repo (RhinoHealth/fcp), one branch (nova/RH-1234), one Jira issue and one Slack thread, until a time. That is the run's scope. The broker answers with a random string, the capability, and the orchestrator writes it onto the VM. From then on, every request from the VM carries the capability, and the broker looks up the scope it stands for.

A valet key is a fair comparison: it starts the car but does not open the trunk, so you can hand it to a stranger. The comparison stops where a capability gets better. A valet key works in any car park, but a capability works only through the broker, which checks every single request against the scope and writes it to an audit log.

read.h: A capability is not a key
p: A key opens a door for whoever holds it, wherever they are. A capability opens nothing by itself. It is 32 random bytes with no meaning inside; only the broker can turn it into a scope, and only for as long as the scope lasts. If an instruction hidden in a ticket makes Nova print it, the attacker gets the power to push nova/RH-1234 through our broker, from inside our network, for less than an hour, with every call logged. That is a small, visible loss instead of a large, silent one.

The broker does not even store the capability. It stores its SHA-256 hash, the way a website stores hashes of passwords: when a request arrives, the broker hashes the capability it carries and looks that hash up. Someone who reads the broker's database learns no capability. When the run ends, the orchestrator revokes the scope, and the same string gets 401 from then on.

notes.text: 32 random bytes, written as 64 hex characters. Nothing in it can be guessed or decoded.
Only the hash is stored, next to the scope: repo, branch, issue, thread and expiry.
Hash what arrived and look it up. An unknown string finds nothing.
Missing or expired means null, and the caller answers 401.

p: Holding the key is only half of the broker's job. A broker that forwards whatever the VM asks, just adding the token, protects nothing: the VM could ask it to push main, and the broker would do it with its own full power. Security people call this a confused deputy, a program with authority that is tricked into using it for someone who should not have it. The cure is to always check the request against the scope of the one who asked.

For git, the broker is a proxy: Nova's git remote points at the broker, not at GitHub. Every push begins with a short list of the refs it wants to change, one line each: the old commit, the new commit and the ref name, for example refs/heads/nova/RH-1234. The broker reads that list before the actual code arrives and refuses anything that is not a normal update of the run's own branch: another branch, a tag, a delete (where the new commit is forty zeros), or a branch that moved since the run's last push, which means a person pushed to it. Only then does the broker add the token and send the same bytes on to GitHub. Pushing for the run, it never asks the VM for anything secret, and it never sends the token back.

notes.text: commands are the ref updates read from the start of the push, before the pack of objects.
Only the run's own branch. main, other branches and tags are all refused here.
A delete is an update whose new commit is all zeros.
If someone else pushed in between, Nova must stop and ask instead of overwriting their work.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the token the broker mints
p: The broker itself never keeps a long-lived GitHub token. It holds the GitHub App's private key and, for each run, asks GitHub for an installation token limited to one repository and a short list of permissions: contents and pull_requests write, checks and actions read. Such a token lives one hour, and the broker refreshes it at 50 minutes.

One permission is never requested: workflows. Without it, GitHub itself refuses any push that changes a file under .github/workflows, so even a perfect broker bug could not let an agent rewrite the CI that judges it. Two more habits come from Byte's broker, which this one started from: a secret guard that replaces any response containing the token or the capability with an error, and an audit line for every allowed and every refused call.

lab.title: A mini broker and a branch that only takes one branch
lab.goal: Run a small broker that gives the VM a capability instead of a key, then make a git remote refuse every push except the run's own branch.

guess.q: An instruction hidden in a ticket comment makes Nova print its capability into the PR, and an attacker copies it to their own laptop. What can they do with it?

options.text: Push to any repo the GitHub App can reach, for an hour.
options.why: That is what a token on the VM would allow. A capability is not a GitHub credential at all; GitHub would not accept it.

options.text: Nothing outside our network; from inside it, only what this one run may do, until the run ends, with every call in the audit log.
options.why: The capability works only through the broker, which still checks the scope, and the broker is not reachable from the internet.

options.text: Read the GitHub App's private key from the broker.
options.why: The capability names a scope. No route ever returns the key, and the secret guard blocks any response that would contain it.

follow.say: Make a folder and write the broker. It keeps a stand-in for the GitHub token, stores only hashes of capabilities, and lets a run push only its own branch.
Start it in the first terminal. It opens one run, prints the capability once, as the orchestrator would hand it to the VM, and shows what it keeps instead.
follow.see:
broker on :8080
capability for nova:RH-1234 (give it to the VM): 09772b0ed37569fa0dd988d4dbeeb5c3a4ec15ba7a137adf374069ec88b453af
what the broker stores: sha256 081343079b84cf7c…
(your capability is different every time)

follow.say: In the second terminal, be the VM. First without the capability, then with it. Copy the 64 hex characters from terminal 1.
follow.do:
curl -s -w ' [%{http_code}]\n' localhost:8080/v1/scope
CAP=<the capability from terminal 1>
curl -s -w ' [%{http_code}]\n' -H "Authorization: Bearer $CAP" localhost:8080/v1/scope

' -H "Authorization: Bearer $CAP" "localhost:8080/v1/push?repo=RhinoHealth/infrastructure&branch=nova/RH-1234"

refused: this run may push only nova/RH-1234 in RhinoHealth/fcp [403]
refused: this run may push only nova/RH-1234 in RhinoHealth/fcp [403]

terminal 1:

audit: REFUSED nova:RH-1234 push RhinoHealth/infrastructure nova/RH-1234

follow.say: Now the git half, with real git. A bare repository stands for GitHub behind the broker, and its pre-receive hook gets exactly the ref list the broker reads: old commit, new commit, ref. Stop the broker with Ctrl+C first; this part needs no server.
Clone it as the VM, make a checkpoint commit on Nova's branch, and push it. The hook prints what it read.
follow.do:
git clone -q github.git vm && cd vm
git switch -q -c nova/RH-1234 && echo "No projects yet" > EmptyCard.txt
git add . && git commit -qm "wip(RH-1234): empty card [skip ci]" && git push origin nova/RH-1234
follow.see:
warning: You appear to have cloned an empty repository.

To /Users/you/academy-labs/scratch/broker-lab/github.git
 * [new branch]      nova/RH-1234 -> nova/RH-1234

git push origin HEAD:main

lab.build: A capability must die with its run. Add a route to broker.mjs: DELETE /internal/runs/<runId> removes every stored scope with that runId and answers "revoked <runId>" (in the real broker this route lives on a separate internal port that only the orchestrator can reach). Restart the broker, copy the new capability, check that /v1/scope answers 200, call curl -s -X DELETE localhost:8080/internal/runs/nova:RH-1234, and ask /v1/scope again with the same capability.
checks: /v1/scope answers 401 without a capability and 200 with the right one.
The push to main and the push to another repo both answer 403, and terminal 1 shows a REFUSED audit line for each.
No answer from the broker ever contains the stand-in token; only the audit line shows its first four characters.
git push to main, a delete and a tag are each rejected with "pre-receive hook declined", and the push of nova/RH-1234 is accepted.
After the DELETE, the same capability gets 401.
lab.fix: Someone simplified the push route to "the broker only needs to know the caller is a real run", and deleted the line that compares repo and branch with the scope. Delete that if block in broker.mjs, restart, and push main with the capability: it answers 200 and the audit says allowed. This is the confused deputy: the broker used its own power for a request it should have refused. Put the check back.
explain: What is the difference between a GitHub token on the VM and a capability on the VM, if both leak?
Why does the broker store sha256 of the capability, and not the capability itself?
What does the broker read from a push before it forwards it, and which three kinds of change does it refuse?
lab.done: The broker refused main and other repos, git refused main, deletes and tags, a revoked capability got 401, and you stopped the broker with Ctrl+C.

check.q: A teammate says: "The broker is just a proxy that adds the GitHub token to the VM's requests." What is missing?

options.text: Nothing; hiding the token is the whole job
options.why: A broker that forwards everything is a confused deputy: the VM could ask it to push main, and it would.

options.text: Caching, so GitHub is called less often
options.why: Caching is not what makes it a wall.

options.text: Checking every request against the run's scope before using the token
options.why: The broker refuses anything outside the scope: another repo, another branch, a delete, a merge. Only then does it add the token.

check.q: Why does the broker keep only the SHA-256 hash of each capability?

options.text: So someone who reads the broker's database still learns no capability
options.why: The broker hashes the capability that arrives and looks the hash up, like a website checking a password.

options.text: Because hashes are shorter than capabilities
options.why: Both are 64 hex characters here. Length is not the reason.

options.text: So capabilities can be decoded later for the audit log
options.why: A hash cannot be decoded, and the audit log records the run, not the capability.

check.q: A push arrives at the broker with the ref update refs/heads/nova/RH-1234, old commit a1b2c3d, new commit forty zeros. What happens?

options.text: It goes through, because it is the run's own branch
options.why: The branch is right, but forty zeros as the new commit means delete.

options.text: It is refused, because a new commit of all zeros deletes the branch
options.why: The broker refuses deletes even on the run's own branch; the branch and its checkpoints must survive the run.

options.text: It is refused, because the old commit is not zeros
options.why: A normal update has a real old commit. The problem is the new one.

p: The broker lives in broker/ in the ai-agents repo and started from Byte's own broker: the capability check, the 1 MiB body limit, /health without auth, the audit log with refused writes, and the secret guard. It runs on inf-rhinohealth as broker.ai-agents.rhinohealth.com, with an internal port only the orchestrator can reach (POST /internal/runs returns the capability, DELETE revokes it) and a sandbox port reached from the VMs over PrivateLink. Scopes are stored as sha256(capability) in Postgres.

The orchestrator writes the capability onto the VM over SSM at the start of each run. A git credential helper in the image reads it, and the remote is https://broker.ai-agents.rhinohealth.com/git/RhinoHealth/fcp.git. The broker mints one-repo, one-hour GitHub App tokens without the workflows permission, and its POST /v1/gh allow-list covers drafts, marking its own PR ready, reading checks and commenting, never merging or approving.

tickets.why: Per-run scopes and capabilities, sha256 storage, one-repo tokens, and the GitHub allow-list.
The git smart-HTTP proxy with checkReceivePack: own branch only, no deletes, stop if the branch moved.
Deploys the broker on inf with its two ports and the hardened container flags.
Narrows CI's Vault access before agents push, because CI runs on an agent's branch outside the broker's control.

words.plain: Our service that holds the GitHub, Jira and Slack credentials and makes those calls for each run, after checking its scope.
A random string that stands for one run's scope. It opens nothing by itself; only the broker can use it.
What one run may touch: one repo, one branch, one Jira issue, one Slack thread, until a time.
A program with power that is tricked into using it for someone who should not have it.
One line at the start of a push: old commit, new commit and ref name. The broker reads these first.

review.q: From memory: the three checks the git proxy makes on every ref update, and the message for each.
review.a: Only refs/heads/<the run's branch> ("Only nova/RH-1234 can be pushed from this run"); no delete, where the new commit is all zeros; and the old commit must equal the run's last push ("someone else pushed, stop and ask").

review.q: Why is it not enough that the capability is random? What else makes a leaked capability nearly worthless?
review.a: It works only through the broker, which is not on the internet; the broker still checks the scope; it expires and is revoked when the run ends; and every call is in the audit log.

review.q: Which GitHub App permission does the broker never request, and what does GitHub do because of that?
review.a: workflows. Without it, GitHub refuses any push that changes .github/workflows, so an agent cannot rewrite the CI that judges it.

remember: The VM holds a capability that means "this run", the broker holds the key, and every request is checked against the run's scope before the key is used.
